name: Lumbar radiculopathy (sciatica)

diagnosisContested.note: The condition itself is accepted, but its label and boundaries are not standardised. A review of 23 prevalence studies found that definitions of sciatica varied widely, only 2 studies used clinical assessment, and prevalence ranged from 1.2% to 43%. A Cochrane diagnostic review found that most physical tests perform poorly in isolation, and a primary-care modelling study used two reference standards, with substantial agreement for one and only fair agreement for the other. Trial populations therefore differ, and a self-reported 'sciatica' in the app may not be true nerve-root pain.

avoidOrModify.movement: Any exercise or activity during which leg pain increases
avoidOrModify.rationale: Participants in a sham-controlled trial were advised to stay as active as possible but to reduce activity if leg pain increased. The advice was given to both arms as part of a package, so its separate effect was not tested. Fritz 2021 shows flares are common even with supervision: 37 of 100 people reported side effects, mostly increased back pain and stiffness. A cohort found that people whose symptoms peripheralised during testing improved about as much as those whose symptoms centralised, so peripheralisation during testing did not predict a poor outcome in that cohort. That finding does not justify training through leg pain, and the peripheralisation group was small.

avoidOrModify.movement: Replacing normal activity with extended bed rest
avoidOrModify.rationale: NICE advises encouraging people to continue normal activities. For sciatica specifically, Cochrane found moderate-quality evidence of little or no difference between advice to rest in bed and advice to stay active (pain SMD -0.03, 95% CI -0.24 to 0.18). Vroomen 1999 found 70% versus 65% improved at 2 weeks (adjusted OR 1.2, 95% CI 0.6 to 2.3), and Hofstee 2002 found neither bed rest nor physiotherapy beat continuing daily activities. This shows rest has no added benefit, not that it harms people with sciatica.

avoidOrModify.movement: Any neural mobilisation in a person with cauda equina lesions, cord signs, or other nervous system pathology such as Guillain-Barre syndrome or multiple sclerosis
avoidOrModify.rationale: The meta-analysis lists these as contraindications and says they should be identified before neural mobilisation. None of its 20 trials reported adverse events, which does not establish safety for self-directed use: Peacock 2023 reports adverse events were not a formal outcome, and Danazumi 2023 states they were not measured.

avoidOrModify.movement: Fixed-direction repeated lumbar flexion or extension applied to everyone with leg pain
avoidOrModify.rationale: The guideline's retained 2012 recommendations describe repeated exercises in a direction determined by treatment response, and it also says flexion exercises can be considered within a combined programme for older people with chronic radiating pain. Fritz 2021 individualised extension progressions to maximise centralisation, while Shacklock 2023 used static flexion with contralateral side bending and walking in a small pilot, and VanGelder 2013, as opinion, avoids flexion in the first phase. The sources therefore do not support a blanket ban or a blanket prescription for either direction.

avoidOrModify.movement: Mechanical spinal traction used to manage leg pain
avoidOrModify.rationale: NICE says not to offer traction for low back pain with or without sciatica, and the JOSPT guideline says physical therapists should not use mechanical traction for chronic low back pain with leg pain (should not, Grade D as inferred from its Table 2). Cochrane found low- to moderate-quality evidence that traction probably has no impact in low back pain with sciatica, with adverse effects in 7 of 32 studies including increased pain and aggravated neurological signs. Thackeray 2016 found no added benefit at any time point. A WHO news release also advises against traction in chronic primary low back pain. NASS rates the evidence insufficient (Grade I), and Vanti 2021 reports a positive supine result drawn from low-quality trials. These address clinical traction and do not assess gym movements such as hanging or inversion.

avoidOrModify.movement: Neural mobilisation as the first step in the acute stage
avoidOrModify.rationale: A 14-member Delphi panel placed information, individualised physical activity and directional preference exercise in the acute stage, and said neurodynamic mobilisation could be added in the sub-acute stage. This is consensus, not trial evidence. George 2021 supports neural mobilisation only for chronic low back pain with leg pain, as a short-term adjunct.

avoidOrModify.movement: Loaded or sustained lumbar flexion, especially lifting with a rounded back and straight knees, or a load held far from the body
avoidOrModify.rationale: No study tested this in people with active sciatica. Indirect support: in one healthy subject, lifting 20 kg gave 2.3 MPa with a round flexed back, 1.7 with flexed knees and 1.1 with the load close to the body; repeated flexion with compression produced herniation in porcine segments, at cycle counts far beyond a gym session; static flexion with compression weakened porcine annulus; and frequently lifting 25 lb or more with straight knees and a bent back was associated with herniation onset (RR 3.95, case-control). VanGelder 2013 avoids flexion and sustained flexed postures in phase I as opinion. Contrary: modelling found stoop lifting had lower compression than squat lifting in healthy people, and a narrative review argues strict neutral may be oversimplified, especially for trained lifters, though it says neutral may suit novices or those with acute pain. Do not read this as a flexion ban.

avoidOrModify.movement: Heavy bilateral lifting such as near-maximal conventional deadlifts during symptoms
avoidOrModify.rationale: No trial tested these lifts in symptomatic lifters, so any restriction is inference. Competition deadlift L4/L5 compression estimates reach 17,192 N, and 75% 1RM gave 7,963 N compression and 1,903 N shear. High-load deadlifts lowered the disc apparent diffusion coefficient, most at L5/S1, as an acute response rather than injury. A hexagonal bar lowered peak lumbar moment in powerlifters; disc load and injury were not reported in the abstract. One case report describes massive L5-S1 extrusion with cauda equina syndrome after a year of training through worsening pain; it cannot show cause. Contrary: Mundt 1993 found weight lifting equipment not associated with lumbar herniation. VanGelder 2013 reintroduces kettlebell and trap bar deadlifts in phase II, starting the kettlebell version at the lightest load possible, as untested opinion.

avoidOrModify.movement: Leg press treated as automatically spine-sparing
avoidOrModify.rationale: In 8 resistance-trained people, peak L4-L5 compression was similarly high across flywheel leg press and squats, and shear was higher in leg press and barbell squat than flywheel squat. This was not a conventional sled leg press, and the participants were resistance-trained rather than people with sciatica, so it removes an assumption rather than setting a limit.

avoidOrModify.movement: Hip-hinge positions with the ankle dorsiflexed, including straight-leg hamstring stretches, when leg symptoms respond
avoidOrModify.rationale: Hip flexion strongly predicted sciatic excursion during forward bending, and force from hip flexion transmits beyond the ankle when it is dorsiflexed. Danazumi 2023 notes hamstring stretching in a home programme could add neural tension. Romanian deadlifts and good mornings were not tested, and no trial of hamstring stretching in lumbar radiculopathy was found, so this is inference from a cadaver study and an in vivo ultrasound study.

avoidOrModify.movement: Long-lying sit-ups, and high-impact loading such as jogging, skipping or trampoline jumping, when leg symptoms respond
avoidOrModify.rationale: Modelling found the highest curl-up forces in long-lying; hook-lying cut shear 46% in men and 39% in women, but compression only 5% and 4%. In vivo data showed high spinal loads during jogging, trampoline jumping and skipping. Neither study tested symptomatic people, so this is load data and not evidence of harm.

avoidOrModify.movement: Lumbar belts or corsets used as treatment
avoidOrModify.rationale: NICE says not to offer belts or corsets for low back pain with or without sciatica, and a WHO news release advises against lumbar braces, belts and supports in chronic primary low back pain. VA/DoD rates the evidence on lumbar supports as insufficient. The passages read do not address a lifting belt during training.

candidateExercises.name: Seated slump slider

dose.frequency: 3 days per week for 2 weeks, with 5 minutes between sets (one small trial, Anikwe 2015, as tabulated in Lin 2023). Another trial, Bhatia 2017, used 5 sets of 15, 5 days per week for 4 weeks.

candidateExercises.cautions: Doses come from small trials where this was added to other treatment. No trial of self-directed mobilisation alone was found, and self-directed use without clinician screening is not established. Excluded if any red flag or listed contraindication applies. Stop if leg symptoms increase. Evidence is very low certainty and conflicts: Sousa Filho 2022 and Plaza-Manzano 2020 found no added benefit, and Ellis 2017 found a slumped position did not change nerve excursion. Do not copy the Shaheen 2025 dose of 100 reps per session with 5-second holds: it was therapist-delivered, and its effects are implausibly large.

candidateExercises.name: Side-lying straight-leg-raise slider

dose.frequency: 3 days per week for 4 weeks; described as repeated 3 times with 10 oscillatory movements (one trial, Colakovic 2013, as tabulated in Lin 2023)

candidateExercises.cautions: Same limits as the slump slider. Added to lumbar stabilisation exercise in the trial. Stop if leg symptoms increase.

candidateExercises.name: Repeated lumbar movement in a direction chosen by symptom response

dose.frequency: Up to 10 reps per direction, as used to test response (Albert centralisation 2012), stopping at once if distal symptoms worsen. Fritz 2021 asked people to do assigned exercises at home every 4 to 5 hours on days between sessions, with reps left to the therapist. No trial tested this exact combination, and direction was chosen by a clinician or algorithm.

candidateExercises.cautions: Results conflict. Symptom-guided exercise beat sham for most outcomes in Albert 2012, and early physical therapy improved ODI by 5.4 points at 6 months in Fritz 2021, but a McKenzie programme matched guideline-based advice at 24 months in a small trial. Direction was set by an algorithm or therapist, which a fixed app routine would not replicate. Evidence from credentialed McKenzie therapists in chronic low back pain (Hennemann 2025) does not transfer directly to self-guided use. In Fritz 2021, 37% of people reported side effects.

candidateExercises.name: Walking

dose.frequency: Not established for sciatica; the opened sources give no dose.

candidateExercises.cautions: Supports staying active rather than treating leg pain. The guideline's walking review covered chronic low back pain, not sciatica, and found no significant differences against other interventions. Walking was part of the Shacklock 2023 pilot package, with no separate dose or effect. Reduce if leg pain increases.

candidateExercises.name: Bird dog

dose.frequency: Home programme in Shaheen 2025: quadruped alternating arms and legs, 2 sets of 10. The frequency of the home sessions was not captured, and it was given to all three arms.

candidateExercises.cautions: This dose comes from one small trial that gave it to all arms, so its own effect was not tested. Choosing this exercise remains expert-opinion mapping onto the guideline's trunk-strengthening and movement-control categories. Reduce if leg pain increases.

candidateExercises.name: Side plank

dose.frequency: Not established; no opened source gives a dose.

candidateExercises.cautions: Choosing this exercise is expert-opinion mapping onto the guideline's broad trunk-endurance category. VanGelder 2013 lists plank progressions and an advanced side plank in phase I without a dose. Reduce if leg pain increases.

candidateExercises.name: Dead bug

dose.frequency: Not established; no opened source names this exercise or gives a dose.

candidateExercises.cautions: Choosing this exercise is expert-opinion mapping onto the guideline's movement-control category. Reduce if leg pain increases.

candidateExercises.name: Cat-cow

dose.frequency: Cat-and-camel exercise in Pradhan 2024: 3 sets of 10, one session a day, 10 sessions in 14 days. Given to both groups of the trial, so its own effect was not tested.

candidateExercises.cautions: Dose comes from one trial that gave it to both groups, so its own effect was not tested. It moves through both flexion and extension, so limit range to what does not increase leg pain.

candidateExercises.name: Self-performed lower-limb neural slider, tolerance dose

dose.frequency: Single session; each slider performed for 30 seconds at about 1 repetition per 3 to 4 seconds, with actual means of 7.3 to 9.5 reps per exercise (Boyd 2017). Tested once, in people with diabetes rather than sciatica.

candidateExercises.cautions: The best-defined self-performed slider dose found, but it comes from a single-session feasibility study in a different population, so it describes tolerance and not benefit in sciatica. That study did not count a stretch that resolved immediately on leaving the position as an adverse event. Excluded if any red flag or listed contraindication applies. Stop if leg symptoms increase.

candidateExercises.name: Side-lying static foramen opening

dose.frequency: Not established; the abstract describes static flexion with contralateral lateral flexion in side-lying but gives no hold time or repetitions.

candidateExercises.cautions: Evidence is one randomised pilot of 20 inpatients, added to forward bending, walking and medication. The Ferreira 2016 trial used passive foramen opening delivered by a therapist. Stop if leg symptoms increase.

candidateExercises.name: Glute bridge

dose.frequency: Home programme in Shaheen 2025: bridging, 2 sets of 10. The frequency of the home sessions was not captured, and it was given to all three arms. VanGelder 2013 lists bridging in phase I without a dose. Pradhan 2024 used bridging at 3 sets of 10 in both groups.

candidateExercises.cautions: Given to all arms of one small trial, so its own effect was not tested. Reduce if leg pain increases.

candidateExercises.name: Pelvic tilt

dose.frequency: Home programme in Shaheen 2025: pelvic tilts, 2 sets of 10. The frequency of the home sessions was not captured, and it was given to all three arms.

candidateExercises.cautions: Given to all arms of one small trial, so its own effect was not tested. Reduce if leg pain increases.

candidateExercises.name: Core bracing

dose.frequency: Home programme in Shaheen 2025: core bracing, 2 sets of 10. The frequency of the home sessions was not captured, and it was given to all three arms.

candidateExercises.cautions: Given to all arms of one small trial, so its own effect was not tested. The STOPS protocol teaches motor control in non-weight-bearing positions first, without stating sets or reps. Reduce if leg pain increases.

candidateExercises.name: Hook-lying abdominal hollowing

dose.frequency: 5-second holds for 5 repetitions, progressing to 30-second holds (VanGelder 2013). Session frequency not given.

candidateExercises.cautions: Level 5 clinical commentary and untested, and it is the only exercise that paper doses. Reduce if leg pain increases.

candidateExercises.name: Goblet squat, later phase only

dose.frequency: Not established. VanGelder 2013 places it in phase II and states that it gives no dosing.

candidateExercises.cautions: Untested expert opinion in athletes with disc herniation. No trial shows when it is safe to start. Not for use while leg symptoms are worsening or any red flag applies.

candidateExercises.name: Trap bar deadlift, later phase only

dose.frequency: Not established. VanGelder 2013 places kettlebell and trap bar deadlifts in phase II and states that it gives no dosing. The lightest-load instruction was found for the kettlebell version, not the trap bar.

candidateExercises.cautions: Untested expert opinion. A hexagonal bar lowered peak lumbar moment in powerlifters; disc load and injury were not reported in the abstract. Not for use while leg symptoms are worsening or any red flag applies.

redFlags.sign: New bladder change with back pain or sciatica: altered urination pattern, hesitancy, frequency, dribbling, incomplete emptying, loss of the sensation of passing urine, retention, or incontinence
redFlags.action: Stop exercising and seek emergency care the same day. UK guidance calls for an urgent same-day MRI based on symptoms alone.

redFlags.sign: Any change in saddle sensation, meaning numbness or tingling in the genital or perianal area
redFlags.action: Stop exercising and seek emergency care the same day. UK guidance calls for an urgent same-day MRI based on symptoms alone.
Stop exercising and go to an emergency department.
Stop exercising and seek urgent medical assessment, because the pathway treats this as potential cauda equina syndrome.

redFlags.sign: Significant or worsening leg weakness, foot drop, or new difficulty walking
redFlags.action: Stop exercising and seek urgent medical assessment.

redFlags.sign: New sexual dysfunction with back pain or sciatica
redFlags.action: Stop exercising and seek urgent medical assessment.

redFlags.sign: New or changed symptoms raising concern for cancer, infection, trauma, or inflammatory disease
redFlags.action: Stop the programme and see a clinician to look for another cause.

redFlags.sign: Back or leg pain that keeps worsening over weeks of training, especially if leg numbness or weakness joins it
redFlags.action: Stop loaded training and see a clinician. Do not train through it.
redFlags.evidenceNote: From a single case report of a person who continued deadlift training through a year of worsening pain. It supports caution and cannot show cause.

redFlags.sign: Severe, disabling leg pain that has not improved with non-surgical care
redFlags.action: See a clinician to discuss referral. Thresholds differ: within 12 weeks in the Danish guideline, 6 to 8 weeks in the Dutch GP standard as relayed by the occupational guideline, and before six months among people whose symptoms warrant surgery in NASS.

limitations: Overall grade is low and the evidence conflicts. Dove 2023 (18 trials, all high or unclear risk of bias) found inadequate evidence to make clinical recommendations on physiotherapy for sciatica, and its pooled effects were null. Both 2025 network meta-analyses report very low confidence and no high-quality evidence that any non-surgical option is superior. Exercise beat advice only slightly for short-term leg pain (low-quality evidence), with no long-term difference (moderate-quality evidence). CONTRADICTIONS. Exercise: NASS rates stand-alone physical therapy or structured exercise as insufficient evidence (Grade I), Khorami finds exercise a could-do (7 guidelines in its table, 6 in its text), Stochkendahl recommends supervised exercise in addition to usual care, a neuropathic pain consensus gives Grade A, and Lewis 2015 found exercise significantly inferior to epidural injection or surgery for overall recovery, on very low validity. Direction-guided work: Albert 2012 and Fritz 2021 are positive, Kilpikoski 2024 is null at 24 months with one advice session matching seven visits, and peripheralisers improved about as much as centralisers in a small group. Neural mobilisation: Lin 2023 reports large pooled effects (pain g -1.097), but 65% of trials were high risk of bias, I2 was about 85-89% and Egger p < 0.001, while Ferreira 2016 was null at its 2-week primary time point, and Sousa Filho 2022, Plaza-Manzano 2020 and Nahid 2025 found no between-group benefit for pain or disability. Nahid 2025 claims superiority its reported between-group result does not support. Baptista 2024 rates all estimates very low. Treatment lasted 6 days to 6 weeks in most reviewed protocols. Shaheen 2025 claims slump beats supine, whereas Ellis 2017 found slump versus upright did not change excursion, and Pourahmadi 2019 suggests non-radicular low back pain may benefit most from slump stretching. Slider excursion ranged from 3.2 to 17.0 mm between Ellis 2012 and Coppieters 2015, and Lin's subgroups favouring sliders over tensioners are not head-to-head. Traction: NICE and George 2021 advise against, NASS and VA/DoD call evidence insufficient, Vanti 2021 is positive in low-quality supine trials, and Cochrane is null. Sitting versus standing: Wilke 1999 and Sato 1999 disagree. Lifting: stoop versus squat modelling and neutral-spine reviews run against common advice, Mundt found no association with weight lifting equipment but an association with bent-back lifting, and those studies concern onset, not recovery. Flexion: Shacklock 2023 and VanGelder 2013 point in opposite directions. Referral timing differs across guidelines (6 to 8 weeks, 12 weeks, before six months). Epidural injection and drug recommendations also disagree (Kreiner 2014, Pangarkar 2019, Stochkendahl 2018, Price 2024) and are outside this exercise record. GAPS. No trial of self-directed neural mobilisation alone was found, and no dedicated Cochrane review of exercise for sciatica was found through a title-only filter. Neural mobilisation is absent from NICE, NASS, VA/DoD, the Saudi and Dutch occupational guidelines, Khorami 2021 and Briggs 2025, which is a null result and not a recommendation against it. No study tested gym lifts, hamstring stretching, sitting limits or Valsalva in symptomatic people, so every lifting restriction here is biomechanical or expert inference from healthy, cadaveric, animal or case data. This absence is not evidence that those lifts are safe. Doses for sliders come from single small trials, usually therapist-delivered and alongside other treatment. No source names dead bug, so it is an expert-opinion mapping with no dose. Side plank is named only in untested commentary without a dose. Bird dog, glute bridge, pelvic tilt, core bracing and cat-cow doses come from co-interventions given to all arms of one small trial each. Exercise recommendations are often for low back pain with leg pain, not confirmed radiculopathy, and Hayden 2021 and Hennemann 2025 are indirect. ACCESS AND READING DEPTH. Not opened: WHO guideline full text (reCAPTCHA), Danish SST guide (HTTP 429), AAPM guideline full text (HTTP 403), KCE Report 287 (HTTP 404), KNGF guideline, and the Cochrane Library directly (HTTP 403). The BMJ 2019 sciatica review could not be opened in the earlier pass and is not used. Corrêa 2022 results were not found. Many sources were abstract only, as accessLevel records, and some full texts were read through summarising fetches or keyword extraction: Dove 2023 (first 100,000 of 155,424 characters), Liu 2023, Lin 2023, Baptista 2024 (first 100,000 of 266,661), VanGelder 2013, STOPS 2011, Delitto 2012, Kreiner 2014 and George 2021. Peacock 2023 doses could not be reopened in the citation check, and one Dove short-term disability subgroup was omitted as internally inconsistent. Grade letters for George 2021 are inferred from its obligation wording and Table 2. Stochkendahl 2018 grades are not reported because the third-party reprint omits the tables. Red flags draw on UK sources, including a local pathway under review and a primary-care article summarising national guidance; the national documents were not opened, and thresholds may differ elsewhere. This is general information for planning exercise around a condition, not diagnosis or treatment.

valuesCorrected: Shaheen 2025 slider volume: 150 to 100 reps per session (10+15+20+25+30).

Pradhan 2024 neurodynamic dose: 3 sets of 10 belonged to the conventional exercises in both groups. The glides were therapist-delivered, 5 glides then 1 minute rest for 5 minutes, 10 sessions in 14 days. Sample corrected from not captured to 58.
Cat-cow: dose changed from not established to 3 sets of 10, because Pradhan 2024 names cat-and-camel, as a co-intervention in both groups.
Side plank: VanGelder 2013 does name an advanced side plank in phase I, still without a dose.
Luites 2022: behavioural treatment is considered after 6 weeks, not 12. Multidisciplinary rehabilitation is the 12-week step.
Luijsterburg 2007: physical therapy vs inactive treatment rests on 1 high-quality trial, not 30.
Lin 2023 table: Morsi 2022 frequency is 3 days per week for 2 weeks. Vijayalakshmi 2022 is slump position, 10 sessions over 3 weeks, with tensioners of 5-7 repetitions of 15-25 seconds.
Khorami 2021: its table lists 7 guidelines each for physical activity and exercise, while its text cites 8 and 6.
Stynes 2018: reference standards differ in agreement, rather than conflict.
Nordberg 2021: higher compression grades were for paracentral herniations; size increased generally.
Neutral spine review: applies to trained lifters; the paper does not say uninjured.
Sjoberg 2023: participants described as resistance-trained, since the abstract does not state symptom status. Ellis 2021: described as in vivo, since the abstract does not state healthy.

Citations: first authors corrected for Hennemann (V), Shinde (AP), Shaheen (HM), Zhu acute (Z), Ferreira protocol (GE), Toribe (A); added for Zhang, Alshanqity, Ramirez, Cherni, von Arx, Hahne (STOPS). Eight missing DOIs added.

Access levels: Todd 2025 and York pathway to full_text. Konstantinou 2008, van der Windt 2010 and Stynes 2018 to abstract_only. Kreiner 2014 to registry_or_summary. NICE NG59, Pangarkar 2019, Peacock 2023 and Danazumi 2023 to not_reconfirmed.
unverifiable: NICE NG59: nice.org.uk returned HTTP 403 and no NICE copy could be opened, so its wording on traction, belts, normal activity, medication and alternative diagnoses was not reconfirmed. The 29 July 2026 update date was seen only in a vendor blog.

Pangarkar 2019, Peacock 2023 and Danazumi 2023: PMC returned a reCAPTCHA page and only abstracts could be read. VA/DoD traction, support, weakness and medication statements, Peacock doses and its 322 total, and Danazumi's adverse event, hamstring and dose statements were not reconfirmed.
Kreiner 2014: the NASS PDF returned no readable text, so grades were confirmed on the Guideline Central summary. The absence of neural mobilisation was not reconfirmed.
Delitto 2012, George 2021, Khorami 2021 and VanGelder 2013 were read through a summarising fetch, and only part of each long page.

Abstract-only sources: anything beyond the abstract, such as Luijsterburg 2008 content, was not rechecked unless its full text is listed as read. Primary slider trials were checked only as tabulated in Lin 2023.
WHO guideline full text and UK national cauda equina documents were not opened.

evidenceGradeRationale: Overall grade stays low. The strongest syntheses disagree or rate certainty very low: Dove 2023 found inadequate evidence for recommendations, and both 2025 network meta-analyses rate their evidence very low. Moderate-quality evidence exists only for narrow points, namely little or no difference between bed rest and stay-active advice, and no long-term difference between exercise and advice. Fritz 2021 is a positive trial with a modest effect.
